textbookText: b. Perigynous flower: The thalamus grows upwardly and form a cup shaped structure. Gynoecium is situated in the centre and other parts of flower are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level. The ovary is half inferior. E.g. rose etc.
c. Epigynous flower: Ovary of a flower is fused with thalamus and other parts of flower are present above the ovary. The ovary is inferior. E.g. sunflower etc.
Figure 2.8.14 Insertion of flower Parts of flower A typical flower consists of four different types of whorls present on thalamus.

1. Calyx: The unit of calyx is called sepal. It is the outermost whorl, generally green in colour (sepaloid) or sometime colourful (petaloid) that protects the flower in bud condition. The sepals may be free (i.e. polysepalous) or fused (i.e. gamosepalous).

2. Corolla : The unit of corolla is called petal. It is variously coloured whorl of flower. Its bright coloured petals attract the insects which help in pollination. The free petals are termed as polypetalous and fused petals are termed as gamopetalous.

Calyx and corolla are accessory organs. In some flowers the calyx and corolla are not distinct and constitute single whorl known as perianth. The unit of perianth is termed as tepal. The mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorls is known as aestivation. Following are the major types of aestivation: a. Valvate – sepals and petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin without overlapping. E.g. Mustard, Custard apple etc. b. Twisted – margin of adjacent sepals or petals overlap regularly. E.g. Hibiscus, Lady finger etc. c. Imbricate – sepals and petals overlap each other but not in any regular manner. E.g. Gulmohar, etc. d. Vexillary – Occurs in pentamerous flower. In this the largest one overlaps the two adjacent which in turn overlap two smallest anterior. It is also known as descending imbricate. E.g. pea, bean etc.

2.8.11 Types of aestivation 3. Androecium: The unit of androecium is called stamen. The stamens in a flower may be free (polyandrous) or united. The united stamens in one bundle (monoadelphous), in two bundles (diadelphous) or in many bundles (polyadelphous). Stamens are sometimes attached to petals known as epipetalous. It is the male reproductive whorl of flower and consists of two parts i.e. anther and filament. The stamens may be syngenesious (i.e. anthers are united together but the filaments remains free) or synandrous (i.e. both anthers and filaments are fused throughout the whole length). Each anther is usually bilobed and each lobe has two chambers, the pollen sacs. The pollen grains are produced in pollen sac. The The attachment of filament to anther lobe may be adnate (filament runs through the whole length of the anther from the base to the apex), basifixed (filament is attached to anther by its base), dorsifixed (filament is attached at the centre to the back of the anther) and versatile (filament attached to the back of the anther at a point only).

4. Gynoecium : The unit of gynoecium is called carpel/pistil. It is the female reproductive whorl of flower and consists of three parts i.e. stigma (receives pollen grains), style (connects ovary and stigma) and ovary (basal swollen ovule containing part). Each ovary bears one or more ovules attached to cushion like structure known as placenta.
Placentation The arrangement of ovules within the ovary is known as placentation. The different types of placentation are:

Axile placentation: placenta is axial (around an axis) and the ovules are attached to it. Ovary is divided into many locules. E.g. tomato, lemon etc. Marginal placentation: Ovary bears longitudinal placenta and the placenta bears one or two rows of ovules. E.g. pea, etc. Parietal placentation: the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on parietal part. Ovary become bi or multilocular due to formation of a false septum. E.g. cucurbita, mustard etc.

Free central placentation: Ovules are borne on central axis and septa are absent. E.g. Dianthus, Primula etc. Basal placentation: a single ovule is borne at the base of unilocular ovary. E.g. sunflower, marigold etc.
Figure 2.8.12 Types of placentation Function of flower
a. Male and female gametes are produced inside respective reproductive structures within a flower that later fuse to form zygote.
b. After fertilization, the ovary develops into fruit. c. Flower provides nectar to attract pollinators like honeybees which later convert it into

honey. d. Petals are brightly coloured and scented to attract animals and insects for pollination that ultimately helps in fertilization. e. Because of brightly coloured petals, human beings cultivate and use flowers for various occasions like wedding, funerals, expressing love etc.
